units.title: Unit 05 — Describing people
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 5. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Describe height and weight using tall, short, of medium height, slim, thin, overweight and fat, and distinguish height, weight and weigh.
Describe hair, eyes, skin and facial hair with have/has (got), using hair as an uncountable noun when appropriate.
Distinguish beautiful, good-looking, pretty, ugly and average-looking, and recognize that some descriptions can be hurtful.
Talk about age with old, young, older, younger, middle-aged and elderly, paying attention to context and politeness.
Ask and answer questions about height, weight, age and appearance using How tall ...?, How much do you weigh?, How old ...? and What does ... look like?.
Describe people in pictures and everyday life, correcting common errors with tall/high and hair/hairs, as practised in exercises 5.1–5.5.

items.example: We asked about the player's height.
items.note: Use tall, not high, to describe a person's height.

items.example: Her weight has stayed the same this year.
items.note: Weight is a noun; weigh /weɪ/ is the corresponding verb.

items.example: My cousin is very tall.
items.note: Use tall, not high, when describing a person's height.

items.example: His younger brother is short.
items.note: Here short refers to height; it also has other meanings in different contexts.

items.example: Her father is of medium height.
items.note: The usual phrase is of medium height, not medium tall.

items.example: My aunt is slim and quite tall.
items.note: Slim is generally more complimentary than thin when describing a person's build.

items.example: He looked thin after being ill.
items.note: Thin can sound less complimentary than slim, depending on the context.

items.example: The vet says our dog is overweight.
items.note: An adjective meaning heavier than is generally considered healthy; use sensitively when describing people.

items.example: The cat is fat, according to the vet.
items.note: Fat can sound offensive when used to describe a person. The unit recommends choosing words carefully.

items.pt: fazer uma dieta; entrar em dieta
items.example: He decided to go on a diet after speaking to a professional.
items.note: The collocation is go on a diet, not go in a diet. Diet can also mean a person's usual food.

items.example: I weigh sixty-five kilos.
items.note: Weigh is the verb; weight is the noun: How much do you weigh?

items.example: My colleague is quite short.
items.note: Quite modifies the adjective. Its strength can vary with context and variety of English.

items.example: Her brother is really slim.
items.note: Really intensifies the adjective; it is also used with many other adjectives.

items.example: The actor has dark skin.
items.note: Use have/has + adjective + skin, for example, she has dark skin. Describe appearance respectfully.

items.example: My sister has dark hair.
items.note: Hair is normally uncountable when referring to all the hair on someone's head: has dark hair, not has dark hairs.

items.example: She has brown eyes.
items.note: Use have/has + adjective + eyes to describe eye colour: she has brown eyes.

items.example: Nina has blonde hair.
items.note: Blonde hair and fair hair are alternatives in this unit. In British English, blonde can describe a person's hair colour.

items.example: He has fair hair and blue eyes.
items.note: Fair hair refers to light-coloured hair; compare fair skin.

items.example: Both children have fair skin.
items.note: Fair describes a light skin tone here; it can also describe light-coloured hair.

items.example: My uncle has blue eyes.
items.note: Place the colour adjective before the noun: blue eyes.

items.example: Maya has green eyes.
items.note: Use the plural eyes when referring to both eyes.

items.example: The singer has a short beard.
items.note: Use has a beard, not is a beard.

items.example: My friend has long hair.
items.note: Hair is normally uncountable in descriptions: she has long hair.

items.example: My teacher has short hair.
items.note: Say he has short hair or his hair is short, not his hair are short.

items.example: My grandfather has a moustache.
items.note: Moustache is the British spelling; mustache is common in American English.

items.example: He has got brown eyes.
items.note: Have got can describe appearance: I've got dark hair; she's got blue eyes. With he/she/it, use has got.

items.example: The portrait shows a beautiful woman.
items.note: An adjective used to describe an attractive appearance; it can also describe things or places.

items.example: Their new neighbour is good-looking.
items.note: Good-looking can describe men or women. Compare What does she look like?, which asks about appearance.

items.example: Her sister is very pretty.
items.note: In this unit, pretty is mainly used to describe girls and women; usage varies by context.

items.example: He called the drawing ugly, which upset the artist.
items.note: Ugly can be hurtful when applied to people; the unit recommends tact.

items.example: The character is average-looking.
items.note: A relatively neutral way to describe someone's appearance as neither especially attractive nor unattractive.

items.example: His hair is dark.
items.note: Say his hair is, not his hairs are, when referring to someone's hair collectively.

items.example: Her skin is very fair.
items.note: Skin occurs with colour adjectives in section B, for example, fair skin.

items.example: Her eyes are green.
items.note: Eyes takes a plural verb: her eyes are blue. Hair normally takes a singular verb: her hair is dark.

items.example: My grandfather is old but very active.
items.note: Elderly may be more polite than old when referring to people, but wording and preferences vary.

items.example: Their daughter is very young.
items.note: The comparative form of young is younger.

items.example: My sister is older than me.
items.note: Older is a comparative adjective: my sister is older than I am.

items.example: Her younger brother is at university.
items.note: Younger is a comparative adjective: my brother is younger than I am.

items.example: The main character is middle-aged.
items.note: Middle-aged describes someone between young adulthood and old age; there is no single fixed age range.

items.example: The centre offers classes for elderly people.
items.note: Elderly can be a more polite description than old in some contexts; avoid stereotyping.

items.example: How tall are you now?
items.note: Ask about height with How tall ...? For a third person: How tall is she?

items.example: How heavy are you, if you don't mind me asking?
items.note: A question about someone's weight. This can be sensitive, so consider the context.

items.example: How much do you weigh at the moment?
items.note: Use the verb weigh after how much: How much do you weigh? Weight is the noun.

items.example: How old is he this year?
items.note: Use How old ...? to ask about age; for example, How old are you?

items.example: What does your new manager look like?
items.note: This asks about physical appearance rather than personality. The pattern is What does + person + look like?

items.example: He is about one point eight metres tall.
items.note: Use a number before metres tall, for example, 1.75 metres tall. Metre is the British spelling.
items.speechText: one point seven five metres tall

units.title: Unit 06 — Health and illness
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 6. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Respond to questions about health using very well, fine, not feel very well, feel ill and feel/be sick, including relevant British English distinctions.
Recognize common health complaints and use headache, toothache and a cold with appropriate expressions.
Understand hay fever, asthma, sneeze and breathe in their unit contexts without treating vocabulary practice as medical diagnosis.
Identify words for tropical and serious illnesses, including mosquito, malaria, cholera, cancer and heart attack.
Avoid got a heart attack; use had a heart attack and recognize the British English expression go to hospital.
Discuss diet, exercise and stress using healthy diet, exercise, swimming, jogging, cycling, relax and panic.
Complete dialogues about symptoms, connect health terms with contextual actions and answer health-related questions, as in exercises 6.1–6.4.

items.example: How are you today, Sam?
items.note: A common question about someone's health or general well-being; replies depend on how the person feels.

items.example: I'm very well this morning, thanks.
items.note: Well describes health in this reply. Compare I feel well with I feel ill.

items.example: I'm fine now, thank you.
items.note: A common positive answer to How are you?, meaning that you are generally well.

items.example: I don't feel very well, so I'll rest today.
items.note: Suggests feeling unwell without necessarily describing a serious illness.

items.example: She feels ill and wants to see a doctor.
items.note: In this unit, feel ill means feel unwell. In British English, sick can also refer specifically to nausea or vomiting.

items.pt: sentir enjoo; sentir-se prestes a vomitar
items.example: The bumpy journey made me feel sick.
items.note: Here feel sick means feel nauseous or feel as if you might vomit; usage can vary between varieties of English.

items.example: I think I'm going to be sick on this boat.
items.note: In British English, be sick may mean vomit. In other contexts and varieties it can mean be ill.

items.example: He began to vomit after the journey.
items.note: Vomit explains the meaning of be sick in this context; it can function as a verb or a noun.

items.example: You should rest after a long day.
items.note: Rest can be a verb or a noun. In the unit, someone who feels unwell goes home to rest.

items.example: The doctor examined the patient.
items.note: A doctor is a medical professional. Get a doctor means find or call for medical help.

items.example: Please get a doctor; she is very ill.
items.note: Get a doctor means find or call a doctor, not purchase one.

items.example: I have a headache after working all day.
items.note: The usual expression is have a headache or have got a headache.

items.example: He has a headache and needs a break.
items.note: Use the article a: have a headache or have got a headache.

items.example: She asked whether there was any aspirin at home.
items.note: A medicine mentioned in the unit's vocabulary example; the sentence is for language study, not medical advice.

items.example: The dialogue mentions taking an aspirin.
items.note: This collocation appears in exercise 6.2. It is a language-learning example, not personal treatment advice.

items.example: My neighbour has toothache.
items.note: In British English, toothache commonly appears without an article: I've got toothache.

items.example: The dentist called me yesterday.
items.note: A dentist treats problems with teeth. The unit connects dentist with toothache.

items.example: I need to go to the dentist next week.
items.note: Use go to the dentist when speaking about a dental appointment.

items.example: He's staying home because he has a cold.
items.note: Have a cold means have a common respiratory illness; cold can also mean low in temperature.

items.example: A cold can make you feel tired.
items.note: A cold is a countable noun for a common illness: I've got a cold.

items.word: go to bed with a hot drink
items.pt: ir para a cama com uma bebida quente
items.ipa: /ɡəʊ tə bed wɪð ə hɒt drɪŋk/
items.example: When he felt unwell, he went to bed with a hot drink.
items.note: A phrase used in the exercise about a cold. It describes the dialogue's context, not a treatment recommendation.

items.pt: rinite alérgica sazonal; febre do feno
items.example: I get hay fever every spring.
items.note: Hay fever is a common name for seasonal allergies; the term does not necessarily mean a person has a fever.

items.example: I often sneeze when there's a lot of pollen.
items.note: Sneeze is a verb and can also be a noun. The source gives the pronunciation /sniːz/.

items.example: Her cousin has asthma.
items.note: Asthma is associated with breathing difficulties in the unit. The written th is not pronounced as in thin.

items.example: It's difficult to breathe in this smoke.
items.note: The final /ð/ in breathe is voiced; compare the noun breath /breθ/.

items.example: A mosquito entered the room.
items.note: The plural of mosquito is mosquitoes.

items.example: There are a lot of mosquitoes near the river.
items.note: Mosquitoes is the plural form used in the unit's discussion of malaria.

items.example: Some mosquitoes can transmit malaria.
items.note: The unit links malaria with mosquitoes in some parts of the world.

items.example: The article discussed cholera and clean water.
items.note: The unit connects cholera with unsafe drinking water.

items.example: The campsite has safe drinking water.
items.note: Drinking water means water intended for people to drink; safe drinking water is free from harmful contamination.

items.example: Researchers are studying new treatments for cancer.
items.note: Cancer is presented as a serious illness. It is not a general word for any health problem.

items.example: My uncle stopped smoking last year.
items.note: Smoke is a verb here, referring to smoking tobacco; smoking is the corresponding -ing form.

items.example: He had a heart attack and was taken to hospital.
items.note: Use have/had a heart attack, not get/got a heart attack, as highlighted in the unit.

items.example: Her neighbour had a heart attack last month.
items.note: The unit illustrates had a heart attack, not got a heart attack.

items.example: The hospital is near the town centre.
items.note: In British English, hospital may appear without the when someone is there as a patient: in hospital.

items.example: She went to hospital after the accident.
items.note: In British English, go to hospital often means go there for medical care; go to the hospital may refer to the building or a specific hospital.

items.example: A healthy diet includes a variety of foods.
items.note: Healthy describes diet. Here diet means a person's usual pattern of eating.

items.example: Her diet includes plenty of vegetables.
items.note: Diet can mean someone's usual food and eating habits, not only a weight-loss plan.

items.example: I exercise before work.
items.note: Exercise can be a verb or noun: Do you exercise? Regular exercise is good for you.

items.example: Swimming is her favourite activity.
items.note: The -ing form names an activity: Swimming is good exercise.

items.example: We go jogging in the park.
items.note: A form of running at an easy pace, mentioned in the unit's exercise dialogue.

items.example: Cycling helps him stay active.
items.note: Riding a bicycle as an activity or sport; another example of exercise in the dialogue.

items.example: Walking regularly can be good for you.
items.note: Good for you expresses a benefit; compare good at, which refers to skill or ability.

items.example: She feels stressed before the presentation.
items.note: Feel stressed describes emotional pressure, not simply having a busy schedule.

items.example: I often feel stressed before exams.
items.note: Use feel + adjective: I feel stressed; she feels relaxed.

items.example: I relax by listening to music.
items.note: The unit suggests relax in a conversation about stress; it means become calmer or less tense.

items.example: Try not to panic about the deadline.
items.note: Use panic about something to name the cause of worry: Don't panic about work.

items.pt: entrar em pânico por causa de; desesperar-se com
items.example: Don't panic about a small mistake.
items.note: Panic about something identifies what causes the anxiety; compare worry about something.

items.example: We usually buy lots of fruit and vegetables.
items.note: The expression comes from the conversation about a healthy diet; lots of means many or much, depending on the noun.

items.example: Are you OK after the journey?
items.note: A question from exercise 6.1 used to check how somebody feels.

items.example: She noticed a mosquito bite on her arm.
items.note: An expression from exercise 6.3, used in the question about an illness associated with mosquitoes.

items.example: Air pollution is a problem in big cities.
items.note: A contextual term from exercise 6.3, connected to air quality and breathing problems.

items.example: Heavy traffic produces fumes near the school.
items.note: A phrase from exercise 6.3 referring to exhaust gases from road vehicles.

items.example: An unhealthy diet may affect your well-being.
items.note: A contrast with healthy diet, used in exercise 6.3; it does not imply a medical diagnosis.

items.example: Smoking is mentioned in the class discussion about health.
items.note: The -ing form is used as a noun for the activity of smoking in exercise 6.3.

items.example: The survey asks whether people get any exercise during the week.
items.note: A phrase from exercise 6.3 contrasting with doing exercise or being physically active.

items.example: Have you ever been in hospital?
items.note: This phrase appears in a personal-experience question in exercise 6.4. In British English, in hospital may omit the when referring to a patient.
